title: Percentages, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we found a percent of a number, and used multipliers for increases and decreases.
In this video, we compute a percent change, undo a discount, and then solve a problem with two changes in a row.
Medium example one. A price rises from eighty dollars to one hundred dollars. What's the percent increase?
The key is the base. Percent change always divides by the original value, which here's eighty, and not by the new value of one hundred.

card.text: The base is the original value

beats.say: The change is the new value minus the old value, so one hundred minus eighty. We divide that by the old value, eighty, and then multiply by one hundred.
One hundred minus eighty is twenty. So the change is twenty out of eighty.
Twenty over eighty is zero point two five, which is one quarter, the fraction of the original that was added.
Multiply by one hundred to get a percent. The increase is twenty-five percent. Dividing by one hundred instead would give twenty percent, which is a common trap answer.
Medium example two. After a fifteen percent discount, a jacket costs sixty-eight dollars. What was the original price?
A fifteen percent discount multiplies the price by zero point eight five. To undo it, we divide by zero point eight five, rather than adding fifteen percent of sixty-eight.
The sale price is the original price times zero point eight five. So the original price is the sale price divided by zero point eight five.
Sixty-eight divided by zero point eight five is eighty. So the original price was eighty dollars.

Hard example. A store marks up the wholesale cost of a jacket by sixty percent. Later, it sells the jacket at twenty-five percent off the marked price, for fifty-four dollars. What was the wholesale cost?
Successive changes multiply. The markup has a multiplier of one point six, and the discount has a multiplier of zero point seven five. We combine them, and then work backward.
Multiply the two multipliers together. This single number tells us the final price as a multiple of the wholesale cost.
One point six times zero point seven five is one point two. So the sale price is one hundred twenty percent of the wholesale cost.
The sale price of fifty-four dollars is one point two times the wholesale cost. To undo that, divide by one point two.
Fifty-four divided by one point two is forty-five. So the wholesale cost was forty-five dollars.
Check by going forward. Forty-five times one point six is seventy-two, which is the marked price. Then seventy-two times zero point seven five is fifty-four, the sale price.
One more idea. Going from forty percent to fifty percent is a ten percentage point increase. But as a relative change, it's ten divided by forty, which is a twenty-five percent increase.
To recap. For percent change, divide by the original value, not the new value.
beats.item: Percent change: divide by the original

beats.say: To undo a change, divide by its multiplier. For successive changes, multiply the multipliers together first.
Check by going forward. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
